# Holt-related witness interview outline and preparation memorandum

你在 Linux Harbor 任务容器中工作，工作目录为 `/app`。五份客户/案件材料位于 `/app/data/input_files/`，不得原地修改。

## 场景与产品边界

Meridian Dynamics, Inc. 已请知识产权诉讼律师团队对 SkyVault Technologies LLC 的指控开展特权保护下的内部事实调查。在准备任何证言前，承办合伙人需要一份访谈计划，说明向各类证人询问什么、每个问题为何重要，以及哪份已提供文件构成事实线索。交付物是访谈设计备忘录，不是已完成证言、诉状、侵权比对表、和解函或实体胜诉意见。

## 任务

1. 制作一份全英文 witness-interview outline memorandum，分为 Dr. Marcus Holt、Meridian technical team 和 Meridian's legal lead 三类证人。每类单列一节，先用两至三个完整句子说明其在本轮访谈中的作用，再列可实际口头询问的问题。
2. 每个问题后均附 `Source:` 和 `Evidentiary purpose:` 注释。引用文件名，并在可得时定位至段落、条款、附件、工作表、`Row #`、工作表行号、事件日期/时区、事件类型、文件名或记录 ID。同一问题依赖多份材料时，说明各来源分别支持哪个命题，不要只堆列文件名。
3. 仅使用下列五份材料作为题包内事实来源。将缺失的人事档案、代码库、开发记录、保全记录、内部沟通、合规材料、完整取证数据和技术比对转化为访谈确认或文件调取问题，不得当作已证实事实。2024 年 3 月 12 日来函本身未提供；不得向其归因超出诉状第 61 段和 2024 年 4 月 5 日回函所记载的内容。
4. 评价材料的实际证明范围：诉状是 SkyVault 的主张；Meridian 回函中的否认、独立开发和合规表述是当事方立场；白皮书是 2022 年的公开技术/营销陈述；ECIAA 是合同与先前发明披露；Exhibit F 是 SkyVault 侧对 `mholt` 账户的选定事件摘录。不得把任一材料的存在直接升级为误用、侵权、独立开发、完整保全、最终授权或技术来源的已定事实。
5. 问题须至少贯通六组 lead families：Holt 的任职与访问历史；Holt 披露的既有工作；PathForge 的开发起点；白皮书的标题与作者信息；DroneNav 及其他公开来源；诉前回函链。对 PathForge 来源的询问应足以区分不同技术模块、贡献者、代码/依赖、测试和发布记录；对公开来源的询问应区分了解、引用、评估、克隆、依赖引入、修改、使用和未使用。
6. 事实需证人确认时使用开放式问法。法务组问题应区分可发现的事实事件与可能受 attorney-client privilege 或 work-product protection 保护的沟通、法律意见和律师思维。
7. 以一段简短建议收尾，说明建议的第一、第二和最后访谈类别，以及该顺序如何用早期访谈和调取结果检验后续证人说法。不预设唯一正确顺序；必须根据特权范围、可用记录、证人知识和交叉核验价值给出可执行理由。

## 关联材料

- `skyvault-complaint.docx`
- `exhibit-f-forensic-log.xlsx`
- `holt-eciaa-agreement.docx`
- `pathforge-whitepaper-excerpt.docx`
- `meridian-cd-response.docx`

## 交付物

仅向 `/app/output/` 提交 `result.docx`：非空、可读、专业法律备忘录格式的全英文 Word 文件。调用 finish 时只报告 `/app/output/result.docx`，不要只在对话中作答，也不要提交脚本、缓存、中间请求、日志或历史版本。

1. Read the five input files in `/app/data/input_files/`
2. Create a witness-interview outline memorandum in English
3. Output to `/app/output/result.docx`

64	[63] E. Dr. Marcus Holt's Employment at SkyVault
65	[64] 42.  Dr. Marcus Holt holds a Doctor of Philosophy degree in Robotics from the Georgia Institute of Technology, which he obtained in 2015. Dr. Holt's doctoral research focused on autonomous navigation and multi-sensor data integration for robotic systems.
66	[65] 43.  SkyVault hired Dr. Holt as a Senior Systems Engineer on June 13, 2016, shortly after SkyVault's founding. Holt remained employed by SkyVault in that capacity until his resignation effective February 16, 2018.
67	[66] 44.  During his approximately twenty-month tenure at SkyVault, Holt had access to SkyVault's most sensitive proprietary technology, trade secrets, and confidential information. Holt's role as a Senior Systems Engineer afforded him broad access to the technical details of SkyVault's AeroCore firmware suite, including its sensor fusion algorithms (TS-1), flight path optimization models (TS-2), drone swarm communication protocols (TS-4), and hardware integration specifications for LiDAR sensor arrays (TS-5). Holt also had access to SkyVault's customer lists and pricing strategies (TS-3) through his participation in customer demonstrations and proposal development.
68	[67] 45.  As a condition of his employment, Holt signed an Employee Confidentiality and Invention Assignment Agreement ("ECIAA") with SkyVault dated June 13, 2016. A true and correct copy of the ECIAA is attached hereto as Exhibit E and incorporated herein by reference.
69	[68] 46.  The ECIAA contains, inter alia, the following material provisions:
70	[69] (a) Section 3 (Confidentiality): Holt agreed to maintain in strict confidence and not to disclose or use, directly or indirectly, for any purpose other than SkyVault's business, any of SkyVault's confidential information or trade secrets during and after his employment. Holt's confidentiality obligations with respect to trade secrets are perpetual in duration. Holt's confidentiality obligations with respect to other confidential information (i.e., confidential information that does not qualify as a trade secret) continue for a period of three (3) years following the date of termination of Holt's employment.
71	[70] (b) Section 5 (Invention Assignment): Holt agreed to assign, and did assign, to SkyVault all of his right, title, and interest in and to any inventions, discoveries, improvements, and works of authorship conceived or reduced to practice during the course of his employment and related to SkyVault's current or reasonably anticipated business.
72	[71] (c) Section 7 (Non-Solicitation): Holt agreed that for a period of twelve (12) months following the termination of his employment, he would not directly or indirectly solicit, recruit, or hire any employee of SkyVault.
73	[72] 47.  Holt was entrusted with SkyVault's most valuable intellectual property and was bound by his obligations under the ECIAA to maintain the confidentiality of SkyVault's proprietary information and to assign to SkyVault any inventions developed during the course of his employment.
74	[73] F. Holt's Departure and Misappropriation
75	[74] 48.  On or about February 9, 2018, approximately one week before his last day of employment at SkyVault, Holt downloaded approximately 4,700 files from SkyVault's internal Confluence workspace onto a personal USB storage device.
76	[75] 49.  On information and belief, this unauthorized download included files containing SkyVault's proprietary sensor fusion algorithms, flight path optimization models, customer lists, swarm communication protocols, and hardware integration specifications — encompassing all five categories of SkyVault's trade secrets (TS-1 through TS-5).
77	[76] 50.  As reflected in the IT forensic log prepared by Hargrove Forensics Group, attached hereto as Exhibit F and incorporated herein by reference, on February 9, 2018, Holt transferred approximately 4,700 files from SkyVault's Confluence workspace to a removable USB storage device. The forensic log identifies the date, time, file count, and destination device associated with the bulk download event.
78	[77] 51.  SkyVault's IT systems recorded the bulk download event on February 9, 2018, and the event was flagged by SkyVault's IT administrator on February 12, 2018.
79	[78] 52.  Holt resigned from SkyVault effective February 16, 2018. Upon his departure, Holt did not return the USB storage device or the files contained thereon to SkyVault, nor did he certify the destruction of any copies of SkyVault's proprietary information in his possession.
80	[79] 53.  Approximately two months after his departure from SkyVault, on or about April 11, 2018, Holt co-founded Meridian Dynamics, Inc. along with Priya Chandrasekaran. Holt assumed the role of Chief Technology Officer at Meridian, a position he holds to this day.

413	[0] PathForge: Next-Generation Autonomous Navigation
414	[1] A Technical Overview of Meridian Dynamics' Autonomous Drone Navigation Platform
415	[2] July 2022
416	[3] Dr. Marcus Holt, CTO and Co-Founder PathForge Engineering Team Meridian Dynamics, Inc.
417	[4] 900 Lakeshore Drive, Floor 12 Austin, TX 78701
418	[5] Document Classification: Public Release / Marketing Technical Paper
419	[6] This document is an excerpt of the full PathForge Technical White Paper (42 pages). This excerpt contains Sections 1–5 and Section 7, omitting detailed hardware specifications (Section 6) and appendices.
420	[8] 1. Executive Summary
421	[9] PathForge is Meridian Dynamics' flagship autonomous navigation platform for commercial unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Developed from the ground up beginning in 2018, PathForge reached commercial launch in September 2020 and has since been deployed by over 60 commercial customers across the logistics, agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and emergency response sectors.
422	[10] Meridian Dynamics, Inc. is a Delaware corporation founded in April 2018 by CEO Priya Chandrasekaran and CTO Dr. Marcus Holt. The company employs 112 people, with a dedicated engineering team of approximately 45 working full-time on PathForge development and customer integration.
423	[11] PathForge is built around three core technology pillars, each addressing a distinct and critical challenge in commercial drone autonomy:
424	[12] 1.  Multi-Sensor Fusion for Real-Time Obstacle Avoidance. PathForge ingests data from LiDAR, stereo vision cameras, inertial measurement units, and ultrasonic sensors, fusing these heterogeneous inputs through an extended Kalman filter framework to produce a unified 3D environmental model that enables real-time obstacle detection and avoidance with sub-40-millisecond latency and positional accuracy within 10 centimeters.
425	[13] 2.  GPS-Denied Environment Navigation. PathForge enables fully autonomous UAV flight in environments where satellite-based positioning is unavailable, degraded, or spoofed, using a visual-inertial odometry approach that combines camera-based feature tracking with IMU data through sliding-window optimization and keyframe-based map management.
426	[14] 3.  Swarm Coordination Protocols. PathForge supports decentralized multi-drone coordination through a mesh-based communication protocol that enables collaborative fleet operations without a central controller, with inter-drone message latency under 20 milliseconds and tested scalability to swarms of 24 drones.
427	[15] Each of these modules addresses fundamentally different technical problems, employs distinct algorithmic approaches, and was developed as an independent component within the PathForge platform. PathForge was built on well-established principles in robotics and autonomous navigation, drawing on decades of academic research in sensor fusion, inertial navigation, and distributed systems. The platform's value lies in its unique integration, optimization, and commercial-grade implementation of these techniques — delivering the reliability, scalability, and certification readiness demanded by enterprise customers in safety-critical drone operations.
428	[17] 2. Introduction and Background
429	[18] The commercial UAV industry has experienced rapid expansion over the past decade, with applications ranging from package delivery and agricultural monitoring to bridge inspection and disaster response. As these applications have grown more sophisticated, so too have the demands on navigation systems. Commercial drone operators require navigation platforms that can function autonomously in complex, dynamic, and often GPS-compromised environments — and they require these platforms to operate with the reliability and safety guarantees that enterprise deployment demands.
430	[19] When Meridian Dynamics began development of PathForge in 2018, the state of the art in autonomous drone navigation was characterized by a rich body of academic research and early open-source implementations, but a scarcity of commercially robust, production-grade platforms that brought these research contributions to market. Dr. Marcus Holt, who holds a PhD in Robotics from Georgia Institute of Technology (2015), led the PathForge architecture design, drawing on his extensive academic background in autonomous systems and a thorough review of the published literature.
431	[20] Several prior works were particularly influential in shaping PathForge's design. In the domain of multi-sensor fusion, the seminal work by Dr. Elena Vasquez, "Multi-Sensor Fusion for Autonomous UAV Navigation," published in IEEE Transactions on Robotics, Vol. 32, No. 5, October 2016, was a foundational contribution establishing the viability of combining LiDAR point cloud data, stereo vision depth maps, and inertial measurement unit (IMU) readings through an extended Kalman filter framework for real-time obstacle detection and avoidance in UAV applications. Vasquez's framework demonstrated that fusing these heterogeneous sensor modalities in real time could achieve obstacle detection latencies below 50 milliseconds with positional accuracy within 15 centimeters, a result that opened the door to practical commercial implementations. Vasquez's work, along with other foundational contributions in Kalman filter design for multi-sensor state estimation (see Nakamura and Okonkwo, 2015), provided the theoretical and empirical grounding for PathForge's sensor fusion architecture.
432	[21] In the domain of GPS-denied navigation, the open-source DroneNav project (GitHub, first committed August 15, 2017) represented an early open-source implementation of visual-inertial odometry for GPS-denied drone flight that demonstrated the feasibility of combining monocular camera feeds with IMU data for position estimation when satellite signals are unavailable. The DroneNav project, while limited to a proof-of-concept implementation, validated key algorithmic approaches to GPS-denied navigation that have since been widely adopted in the academic and commercial UAV communities, including sliding-window optimization and keyframe-based map management. DroneNav's publicly available codebase provided a valuable reference point for the broader community and informed numerous subsequent research efforts and commercial implementations.
433	[22] PathForge was designed to bring these well-known academic and open-source concepts into a commercially robust, production-grade platform with the reliability, scalability, and certification readiness demanded by enterprise customers. The sections that follow describe each of PathForge's three core technology modules in technical detail, articulating both the established principles on which they are built and the engineering contributions that make PathForge suitable for real-world commercial deployment.
434	[24] 3. Multi-Sensor Fusion for Real-Time Obstacle Avoidance
435	[25] 3.1 Architecture Overview
436	[26] PathForge's multi-sensor fusion subsystem is the foundation of its real-time obstacle avoidance capability. The subsystem ingests data from multiple heterogeneous sensor types simultaneously, fusing these data streams into a unified environmental model that supports continuous autonomous flight in cluttered and dynamic environments.
437	[27] The sensor suite comprises the following modalities:
438	[28] •  LiDAR Sensor Arrays. PathForge integrates 360-degree scanning LiDAR units providing three-dimensional point cloud data at update rates of 20 Hz, with an effective detection range of up to 120 meters. LiDAR provides high-accuracy range measurements that form the backbone of the environmental model, particularly for detecting obstacles at medium to long range.
439	[29] •  Stereo Vision Cameras. Dual-camera pairs provide depth maps via stereo disparity computation at 30 frames per second, with an effective range of 0.5 to 30 meters. Stereo vision complements LiDAR by providing dense depth information at close to medium range and enabling visual texture analysis for obstacle classification.
440	[30] •  Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU). A 6-axis IMU comprising a 3-axis accelerometer and a 3-axis gyroscope provides high-frequency pose estimation data at 200 Hz. The IMU serves as the primary source of short-term motion estimation, bridging the gaps between the lower-frequency LiDAR and camera updates and providing continuous attitude and acceleration measurements.
441	[31] •  Ultrasonic Proximity Sensors. Short-range ultrasonic sensors with a detection envelope of 0 to 5 meters provide close-quarters obstacle detection for final-approach maneuvering, landing, and operations in confined spaces.
442	[32] PathForge employs an extended Kalman filter (EKF) framework to fuse these sensor data streams into a unified environmental model. The EKF processes LiDAR point clouds, stereo vision depth maps, and IMU readings to produce a real-time three-dimensional occupancy grid representing the drone's surrounding environment. The filter's state vector incorporates the UAV's position, velocity, orientation, and sensor-specific biases, with measurement updates from each sensor modality incorporated according to sensor-specific noise covariance matrices that reflect each sensor's accuracy characteristics and failure modes.
443	[33] The sensor fusion pipeline runs on a dedicated onboard processing module with a target obstacle detection latency of under 40 milliseconds and positional accuracy of within 10 centimeters in structured environments. This architecture — combining LiDAR, stereo vision, and IMU data through an extended Kalman filter framework for real-time UAV obstacle avoidance — follows the general approach established by Vasquez (2016) and represents a commercially optimized implementation of that foundational methodology.
444	[34] 3.2 Obstacle Detection and Avoidance Pipeline
445	[35] The PathForge obstacle detection and avoidance pipeline operates as a continuous processing loop, executing the following sequential stages on each cycle:
446	[36] Step 1 — Sensor Data Acquisition. Raw data is collected simultaneously from LiDAR arrays (20 Hz), stereo cameras (30 fps), IMU (200 Hz), and ultrasonic sensors (40 Hz) at their respective native update rates. Each sensor's output is buffered in a per-sensor input queue on the processing module.
447	[37] Step 2 — Temporal Alignment and Synchronization. Timestamps from each sensor stream are aligned using a hardware clock synchronization protocol to ensure all readings used in a given fusion cycle correspond to the same moment in time. The synchronization protocol compensates for sensor-specific latencies and communication delays, achieving temporal alignment within 500 microseconds across all sensor modalities.
448	[38] Step 3 — Pre-Processing and Noise Filtering. Individual sensor data streams undergo noise reduction, outlier rejection, and calibration correction before fusion. LiDAR point clouds are filtered to remove ground-plane returns and spurious reflections. Stereo depth maps are filtered for disparity outliers and occlusion artifacts. IMU readings are corrected for known bias and scale factor errors using online calibration estimates.
449	[39] Step 4 — Extended Kalman Filter Fusion. The EKF state vector incorporates UAV position (3D), velocity (3D), orientation (quaternion), accelerometer biases (3D), and gyroscope biases (3D). Measurement updates from each sensor modality are incorporated sequentially within each cycle. Each sensor's measurement model maps the state vector to predicted sensor outputs, and the difference between predicted and actual measurements drives the state correction. Sensor-specific noise covariance matrices weight each modality according to its estimated reliability.
450	[40] Step 5 — 3D Occupancy Grid Generation. Fused data is projected into a voxelized three-dimensional grid representing the probability of occupancy at each point in the UAV's local coordinate frame. The grid is updated incrementally, with new observations merged into the existing grid using Bayesian occupancy update rules.
451	[41] Step 6 — Obstacle Classification and Tracking. Detected obstacles are classified as static or dynamic based on temporal consistency analysis across successive occupancy grid updates. For dynamic obstacles, velocity vectors are estimated using a multi-frame tracking algorithm, enabling prediction of future obstacle positions for collision assessment.
452	[42] Step 7 — Avoidance Path Computation. If an obstacle is detected on or near the planned trajectory, a rapid replanning algorithm generates an avoidance maneuver within the UAV's dynamic flight envelope. The replanning algorithm optimizes for minimum deviation from the planned path while maintaining safety margins around all detected obstacles.
453	[43] The entire pipeline executes in a continuous loop, enabling real-time obstacle avoidance during autonomous flight. This pipeline architecture follows the general approach established in the academic literature on multi-sensor fusion for autonomous UAV navigation. In particular, the core fusion methodology — heterogeneous sensor inputs processed through an extended Kalman filter to produce a 3D environmental model for obstacle avoidance — directly implements the framework described by Vasquez (2016), adapted and optimized for commercial-grade reliability and performance.
454	[44] 3.3 Performance Benchmarks
455	[45] PathForge's multi-sensor fusion module has been extensively tested across a range of flight conditions and environments. The following performance benchmarks were recorded during standardized testing at Meridian Dynamics' flight test facility and at customer deployment sites:
456	[47] These results represent meaningful improvements over the baseline performance reported in the academic literature, including Vasquez (2016), who demonstrated 47 milliseconds detection latency and 15 centimeters positional accuracy in controlled laboratory conditions. PathForge achieves a 19% improvement in detection latency and a 47% improvement in positional accuracy in structured environments, reflecting the engineering investment in commercial-grade sensor calibration, noise modeling, and processing pipeline optimization. In unstructured environments, PathForge's 14 cm RMS accuracy is comparable to Vasquez's laboratory results, reflecting the inherent difficulty of operating in cluttered, unpredictable conditions. These benchmarks confirm that PathForge's approach — building upon the foundational EKF-based multi-sensor fusion methodology established in the academic literature — delivers production-ready performance suitable for safety-critical commercial drone operations.
457	[49] 4. GPS-Denied Environment Navigation
458	[50] 4.1 Problem Statement
459	[51] Reliable position estimation is essential for autonomous UAV flight, yet satellite-based positioning systems such as GPS are frequently unavailable, degraded, or unreliable in critical operational environments. Urban canyons create multipath interference and signal blockage. Indoor environments — warehouses, tunnels, parking structures — lack satellite visibility entirely. Dense tree canopy attenuates signals below usable thresholds. In contested electromagnetic environments, GPS signals may be jammed or spoofed, creating hazardous position errors.
460	[52] PathForge's GPS-denied navigation module enables autonomous UAV flight without reliance on any satellite-based positioning system. The module produces continuous, drift-corrected position and orientation estimates using onboard sensors alone, enabling the UAV to navigate, execute mission plans, and return to base entirely without GPS input. This capability has been a subject of active academic and open-source research for over a decade, with significant prior work including the DroneNav open-source project (2017), which demonstrated the viability of visual-inertial odometry for GPS-denied drone flight.
461	[53] 4.2 Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) Approach
462	[54] PathForge's GPS-denied navigation is based on visual-inertial odometry (VIO), an approach that combines camera-based visual motion estimation with inertial measurement data to produce continuous position and orientation estimates without external references. The system combines two primary sensor inputs:
463	[55] •  Monocular or Stereo Camera Feeds. Visual cameras provide image sequences from which relative motion can be estimated by tracking visual features across frames. PathForge supports both monocular and stereo camera configurations, with stereo preferred for its ability to recover absolute scale directly from disparity measurements.
464	[56] •  IMU Data. The 6-axis inertial measurement unit provides high-frequency (200 Hz) acceleration and angular rate measurements that capture the UAV's motion between camera frames, providing motion priors that constrain and stabilize the visual estimation.
465	[57] The algorithmic pipeline for PathForge's VIO module comprises the following core components:
466	[58] Feature Extraction and Tracking. Visual features — corners, edges, and other salient image structures — are extracted from each camera frame using a feature detection algorithm and tracked across successive frames to estimate inter-frame camera motion. Feature correspondences between frames provide the geometric constraints from which the UAV's trajectory is estimated.
467	[59] Sliding-Window Optimization. Rather than maintaining a full history of all observations (which would be computationally intractable for real-time operation), the system maintains a sliding window of recent keyframes and optimizes the UAV's pose trajectory within this window. This approach balances computational efficiency with estimation accuracy, retaining sufficient historical context to constrain the current pose estimate while bounding processing time.
468	[60] Keyframe-Based Map Management. As the UAV navigates, selected frames are designated as keyframes and used to build a sparse environmental map. The system includes loop closure detection, which identifies when the UAV returns to a previously visited location, enabling correction of accumulated position drift by recognizing previously mapped features.
469	[61] IMU Pre-Integration. IMU measurements between camera frames are pre-integrated into relative motion constraints that provide strong motion priors for the optimization. Pre-integration avoids the need to re-linearize IMU measurements when the state estimate changes, improving computational efficiency.
470	[62] This approach is well-established in the robotics community. Open-source implementations such as the DroneNav project (2017) have demonstrated the viability of sliding-window VIO for GPS-denied UAV flight. DroneNav's publicly available codebase implemented the core pipeline of feature tracking, sliding-window optimization, keyframe management, and IMU pre-integration for monocular camera configurations.
471	[63] PathForge builds upon these established techniques with several engineering improvements designed for commercial robustness: (1) multi-scale feature tracking that maintains tracking accuracy in low-texture environments where standard feature detectors fail, (2) adaptive keyframe selection based on information gain rather than fixed temporal or spatial intervals, ensuring that keyframes are placed where they provide the greatest localization benefit, and (3) tightly-coupled LiDAR-VIO fusion as a fallback mode that incorporates LiDAR range measurements directly into the VIO optimization when visual features are insufficient, such as in featureless corridors or low-light conditions.
472	[64] 4.3 Adaptive Flight Path Optimization
473	[65] In GPS-denied environments, position uncertainty is not constant — it varies with the availability and quality of visual features, the UAV's motion dynamics, and the accumulated duration of GPS-denied flight. PathForge addresses this challenge with an adaptive flight path optimization algorithm that integrates real-time localization uncertainty into mission-level planning.
474	[66] The system continuously re-plans its trajectory based on the VIO-generated position estimate and the sparse map maintained by the keyframe manager. The adaptive path optimization algorithm balances mission objectives — reaching waypoints, completing survey patterns, maintaining coverage schedules — against navigation uncertainty. When the position uncertainty estimate grows (for example, when the UAV transits a featureless corridor or operates in degraded lighting), the algorithm biases the trajectory toward feature-rich areas where visual localization accuracy can be restored, even if this requires a temporary deviation from the optimal geometric path.
475	[67] The algorithm additionally incorporates battery constraints, ensuring that the UAV retains sufficient energy to return to a known location before power is exhausted. Obstacle data from the sensor fusion module (Section 3) is integrated directly into the path planner, ensuring that avoidance maneuvers and GPS-denied navigation operate cooperatively. Mission priority parameters allow operators to configure the balance between mission completion aggressiveness and navigation conservatism based on operational requirements.
476	[68] Adaptive flight path optimization in GPS-denied environments is an area of active research in the autonomous systems community. PathForge's implementation extends the foundational VIO-based navigation demonstrated in projects like DroneNav by integrating mission-level planning with real-time localization uncertainty, creating a closed-loop system in which the navigation module's confidence directly informs the flight planner's decisions.
477	[69] 4.4 Performance in GPS-Denied Conditions
478	[70] PathForge's GPS-denied navigation module has been tested extensively across multiple GPS-denied environment types, including warehouse interiors, utility tunnels, and dense urban canyon corridors. The following performance benchmarks were recorded during standardized testing:
479	[72] Testing environments included a 10,000 sq. ft. warehouse facility, a 1.2-kilometer utility tunnel, and a simulated urban canyon course with building separations of 8–15 meters. These results confirm that PathForge's VIO-based GPS-denied navigation delivers production-grade reliability suitable for commercial deployment in satellite-denied operational environments.
480	[74] 5. Swarm Coordination Protocol
481	[75] 5.1 Overview.  PathForge's swarm coordination capability enables multiple drones running the PathForge platform to operate collaboratively as a coordinated fleet. The swarm module was developed beginning in 2019, with first production deployment in early 2021. The core concept is a decentralized coordination protocol in which each drone in the swarm shares position, status, and intent information with neighboring drones via a low-latency mesh communication network, without requiring a central controller or ground station to mediate coordination decisions. The protocol enables collaborative task execution, formation flying, distributed area coverage, and inter-drone collision avoidance across heterogeneous drone fleets operating in shared airspace.
482	[76] 5.2 Communication Architecture
483	[77] The swarm communication system is built on the following architectural components:
484	[78] Mesh Networking. Each drone acts as a node in a wireless mesh network, communicating with nearby drones using a dedicated radio link operating on 900 MHz or 2.4 GHz frequency bands, selectable based on operational requirements and regulatory constraints. The mesh topology ensures that the network is resilient to individual node failures — if one drone loses connectivity, neighboring drones automatically re-route communications through alternative paths. Each drone communicates directly only with drones within its radio range, and multi-hop routing extends effective communication range across the full swarm.
485	[79] Low-Latency Message Protocol. PathForge uses a custom lightweight message protocol specifically optimized for UAV swarm applications. The protocol minimizes serialization overhead and transmission latency, with a target inter-drone message latency of under 20 milliseconds for position and intent broadcasts. Messages are compact binary-encoded packets containing position, velocity, heading, battery status, planned trajectory waypoints, and mission state information.
486	[80] Heartbeat and Status Broadcasts. Each drone periodically broadcasts its current state to all drones within communication range at a rate of 10 Hz. These heartbeat broadcasts enable every drone to maintain a real-time picture of its neighbors' positions, velocities, headings, battery levels, and planned trajectories. The loss of heartbeat signals from a neighbor triggers a timeout protocol that adjusts swarm behavior to account for the missing member.
487	[81] Decentralized Consensus. When coordination decisions are needed — such as task allocation, formation changes, area partitioning, or collision avoidance between swarm members — the protocol uses a lightweight consensus algorithm that converges within three message rounds among participating drones. This algorithm enables the swarm to reach agreement on shared decisions without any central arbitrator, distributing both the computation and the decision authority across all swarm members.
488	[82] The protocol design draws on well-established principles from distributed systems and mobile ad hoc networking (MANET) literature. Decentralized drone swarm coordination has been an active area of research, with numerous academic publications and open-source projects exploring mesh-based communication and consensus protocols for multi-robot systems (see Ferreira et al., 2016).
489	[83] 5.3 Collision Avoidance Between Swarm Members
490	[84] Preventing collisions between drones operating in the same swarm is a safety-critical function of the coordination protocol. Each drone maintains a predicted trajectory for all neighbors within communication range, extrapolated from the most recently received heartbeat broadcasts. A conflict detection algorithm continuously evaluates whether any pair of predicted trajectories comes within a defined safety margin (configurable, default 3 meters).
491	[85] If a potential conflict is detected, the protocol triggers a priority-based deconfliction procedure. Each drone in the swarm is assigned a static priority index at mission start. When two drones detect a mutual trajectory conflict, the drone with the lower priority index adjusts its trajectory to resolve the conflict, while the higher-priority drone continues on its planned path. The deconfliction computation runs locally on each drone, requiring no central arbitrator, and the resolution maneuver is computed and executed within one planning cycle (typically under 100 milliseconds from conflict detection to maneuver initiation).
492	[86] 5.4 Scalability and Performance
493	[87] The swarm coordination module has been tested in field conditions with the following results:
494	[89] The sub-linear scaling behavior is a consequence of the mesh topology, which limits each drone's broadcast scope to its local neighborhood rather than requiring communication with every drone in the swarm. This architectural choice ensures that adding drones to the swarm does not proportionally increase the communication burden on each individual drone.
495	[90] The swarm coordination module is one of multiple distinct technology components in the PathForge platform, alongside the multi-sensor fusion module, the GPS-denied navigation module, the analytics dashboard, and the hardware integration layer. Each module addresses different technical problems, employs distinct algorithms and communication paradigms, and was developed as an independent engineering effort within the broader PathForge program.
496	[92] 6. Hardware Integration Specifications
497	[93] [Section 6 — Hardware Integration Specifications — omitted from this excerpt. The full white paper contains detailed specifications for PathForge's hardware abstraction layer, supported sensor hardware models, and drone platform integration guides.]
498	[95] 7. Platform Architecture and Modularity
499	[96] 7.1 Modular Design Philosophy
500	[97] PathForge is designed as a modular platform consisting of multiple distinct technology components that can be licensed and deployed independently or together, depending on customer requirements:
501	[98] 1.  Navigation Module — encompasses the multi-sensor fusion capabilities (Section 3) and the GPS-denied navigation capabilities (Section 4), providing the core autonomous flight functionality.
502	[99] 2.  Swarm Coordination Module — the decentralized swarm protocol described in Section 5, enabling multi-drone collaborative operations.
503	[100] 3.  Analytics Dashboard — a cloud-based mission planning and post-flight analytics tool that provides operators with flight telemetry visualization, mission performance metrics, and fleet management capabilities.
504	[101] 4.  Hardware Integration Layer — an abstraction layer that provides compatibility with diverse drone hardware platforms and sensor configurations, enabling PathForge to run on a range of commercial drone frames and sensor suites.
505	[102] These modules are independently developed, independently deployable, and independently priced. Customers may purchase only the modules relevant to their operational requirements. A logistics operator performing single-drone warehouse inspections may license only the Navigation Module, while a large-scale agricultural survey operation may license the Navigation Module, Swarm Coordination Module, and Analytics Dashboard together.
506	[103] The Navigation Module represents the core of PathForge's value proposition, accounting for the largest share of customer deployments. The Swarm Coordination Module, Analytics Dashboard, and Hardware Integration Layer are optional add-on components that extend the platform's capabilities for customers with more complex operational needs. Each module addresses fundamentally different technical domains — sensor fusion and localization, distributed coordination and communication, data analytics and visualization, and hardware abstraction — and each was engineered as a self-contained component with well-defined interfaces.
507	[104] 7.2 Technology Provenance and Development Timeline
508	[105] PathForge's development followed a phased timeline corresponding to the complexity and maturity of each technology module:
509	[106] •  April 2018: Meridian Dynamics, Inc. incorporated in Delaware. PathForge development begins under Dr. Marcus Holt's technical leadership.
510	[107] •  Q3 2018 – Q4 2019: Multi-sensor fusion module designed and prototyped. The architecture was informed by extensive review of published academic literature, including Vasquez (2016) and other foundational works in sensor fusion for autonomous navigation such as Nakamura and Okonkwo (2015). Iterative prototyping and testing refined the EKF implementation, sensor calibration pipeline, and occupancy grid algorithms for commercial-grade reliability.
511	[108] •  Q1 2019 – Q3 2020: GPS-denied navigation module developed. Design informed by academic visual-inertial odometry research and publicly available implementations including the DroneNav open-source project (2017). PathForge's VIO pipeline was developed independently, drawing on the same well-known algorithmic foundations — sliding-window optimization, keyframe-based mapping, IMU pre-integration — while adding the multi-scale feature tracking, adaptive keyframe selection, and LiDAR-VIO fusion capabilities required for commercial deployment.
512	[109] •  Q2 2019 – Q1 2021: Swarm coordination protocol designed and tested. Protocol design based on published distributed systems and MANET research, including consensus algorithms for multi-robot coordination (Ferreira et al., 2016).
513	[110] •  September 2020: PathForge v1.0 commercial launch, initially comprising the Navigation Module and Hardware Integration Layer.
514	[111] •  2021–2022: Continued platform enhancements, expansion of customer base to over 60 commercial operators, Swarm Coordination Module production deployment (Q1 2021), Analytics Dashboard release (Q3 2021).
515	[112] All PathForge technology was developed independently by the Meridian engineering team. The platform builds upon publicly available academic research and open-source implementations that are widely known in the autonomous systems community. Meridian's engineering contribution lies in the rigorous optimization, integration, testing, and commercial hardening required to transform well-established research concepts into a production-grade platform suitable for safety-critical commercial UAV operations.
516	[114] 8. Conclusion
517	[115] PathForge is a commercially proven autonomous navigation platform built on well-established academic and open-source foundations, optimized for the reliability and scalability that commercial drone operators demand. Its three core technology pillars — multi-sensor fusion for real-time obstacle avoidance (99.7% detection rate, 38 ms latency, 8 cm accuracy), GPS-denied environment navigation (< 0.5% drift, 97.3% mission success), and decentralized swarm coordination (14 ms inter-drone latency, zero collisions across 1,200+ hours) — provide a comprehensive autonomous flight capability for enterprise UAV deployments.
518	[116] Meridian Dynamics continues to invest in PathForge development, with active research and engineering programs expanding each technology module's capabilities and extending platform compatibility to new drone hardware and sensor configurations. We welcome collaboration with the broader UAV and robotics research community and are committed to advancing the state of commercial autonomous navigation.
519	[117] For further information, please contact:
520	[118] Meridian Dynamics, Inc. 900 Lakeshore Drive, Floor 12 Austin, TX 78701

8	[7] 1.  SkyVault is a pioneer in unmanned aerial vehicle ("UAV") flight control and autonomous navigation technology. Since its founding in 2016, SkyVault has invested millions of dollars and thousands of engineering hours developing its proprietary "AeroCore" firmware suite, sensor fusion algorithms, flight path optimization models, drone swarm communication protocols, and related technologies. SkyVault holds a portfolio of fourteen (14) United States utility patents covering its innovative UAV technologies, including the three patents asserted in this action.
9	[8] 2.  SkyVault's former employee, Dr. Marcus Holt ("Holt"), who served as a Senior Systems Engineer at SkyVault from June 2016 to February 2018, departed SkyVault and co-founded Meridian Dynamics, Inc. approximately two months later. On information and belief, Holt used SkyVault's proprietary technology, patented inventions, and copyrighted firmware code to build Meridian's competing "PathForge" autonomous navigation platform. PathForge directly competes with SkyVault's products in the commercial drone market, and its technical architecture bears unmistakable hallmarks of SkyVault's proprietary innovations.
10	[9] 3.  SkyVault brings this action to remedy Meridian's ongoing infringement of three SkyVault utility patents, misappropriation of SkyVault's valuable trade secrets, infringement of SkyVault's copyrighted AeroCore firmware, breach of the confidentiality and invention assignment agreement between SkyVault and Holt, and related wrongful conduct. Meridian's unlawful conduct has caused and continues to cause substantial and irreparable harm to SkyVault's business, competitive position, and intellectual property rights. SkyVault seeks injunctive relief, compensatory damages, enhanced damages, exemplary damages, attorneys' fees, and all other relief to which it may be entitled.
11	[10] I. THE PARTIES
12	[11] A. Plaintiff SkyVault Technologies LLC
13	[12] 4.  Plaintiff SkyVault Technologies LLC is a limited liability company organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware, formed on January 8, 2016. SkyVault maintains its principal place of business at 4100 Innovation Parkway, Suite 220, Plano, Texas 75024.
14	[13] 5.  SkyVault was founded by Dr. Rajan Mehta ("Dr. Mehta"), a former aerospace engineer with over twenty years of experience in avionics, guidance systems, and autonomous vehicle technologies. Dr. Mehta established SkyVault with the vision of developing next-generation proprietary UAV flight control systems and autonomous navigation solutions for the rapidly growing commercial drone market.
15	[14] 6.  Since its founding, SkyVault has developed a suite of proprietary UAV technologies, including its flagship "AeroCore" firmware suite, which provides comprehensive flight control, sensor fusion, path optimization, and swarm coordination capabilities for commercial drone platforms. SkyVault's AeroCore technology is recognized in the industry as a leading solution for autonomous UAV operations.
16	[15] 7.  SkyVault holds a portfolio of fourteen (14) United States utility patents related to drone guidance, sensor fusion, autonomous navigation, and related technologies, including the three patents asserted in this action. SkyVault's patent portfolio reflects years of sustained investment in research and development.
17	[16] 8.  For fiscal year 2023, SkyVault generated approximately $8.2 million in annual revenue. SkyVault employs approximately thirty-four (34) engineers, scientists, and other professionals at its Plano, Texas headquarters who are dedicated to the continued development, commercialization, and support of SkyVault's proprietary UAV technologies.
18	[17] B. Defendant Meridian Dynamics, Inc.
19	[18] 9.  Defendant Meridian Dynamics, Inc. is a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware, formed on April 11, 2018. Meridian maintains its headquarters at 900 Lakeshore Drive, Floor 12, Austin, Texas 78701.
20	[19] 10.  Meridian was co-founded by Chief Executive Officer Priya Chandrasekaran and Chief Technology Officer Dr. Marcus Holt. As alleged more fully herein, Dr. Holt is a former SkyVault employee who had extensive access to SkyVault's most sensitive proprietary technology, trade secrets, and confidential information during his employment at SkyVault.
21	[20] 11.  Meridian develops and commercializes the "PathForge" autonomous navigation platform for commercial drones. PathForge provides multi-sensor fusion, GPS-denied navigation, and drone swarm coordination capabilities that directly compete with SkyVault's AeroCore-based products.
22	[21] 12.  On information and belief, Meridian employs approximately 112 people. In March 2023, Meridian raised a $35 million Series B funding round led by Ridgepoint Ventures. On information and belief, Meridian generated approximately $19.4 million in revenue for fiscal year 2023. On information and belief, Meridian has generated in excess of $50 million in cumulative revenue from its PathForge platform since its launch in September 2020.
23	[22] II. JURISDICTION
24	[23] 13.  This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over the patent infringement claims (Counts I, II, and III) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1338(a) because those claims arise under the patent laws of the United States, 35 U.S.C. § 1 et seq., including 35 U.S.C. § 271.
25	[24] 14.  This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over the federal trade secret misappropriation claim (Count IV) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1331 because that claim arises under the Defend Trade Secrets Act of 2016 ("DTSA"), 18 U.S.C. § 1836 et seq.
26	[25] 15.  This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over the copyright infringement claim (Count VI) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1338(a) because that claim arises under the Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 101 et seq., including 17 U.S.C. § 501.
27	[26] 16.  This Court has supplemental jurisdiction over the state-law claims (Count V — Texas Uniform Trade Secrets Act; Count VII — Breach of Contract; Count VIII — Unjust Enrichment; Count IX — Unfair Competition) pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) because those claims arise out of the same case or controversy as the federal claims and are so related to the federal claims that they form part of the same case or controversy under Article III of the United States Constitution.
28	[27] 17.  This Court has personal jurisdiction over Meridian. Meridian is a Delaware corporation that is headquartered in Austin, Texas, and that conducts substantial business throughout the State of Texas. Meridian has committed acts of patent infringement, trade secret misappropriation, copyright infringement, and related unlawful conduct within the State of Texas and within the Eastern District of Texas. Meridian has purposefully directed its infringing and wrongful activities toward and within the Eastern District of Texas, including by selling and offering for sale the PathForge platform to customers located in the Eastern District of Texas. The exercise of jurisdiction over Meridian comports with the requirements of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
29	[28] III. VENUE
30	[29] 18.  Venue is proper in this judicial district under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b) because Plaintiff SkyVault is registered to do business in the Eastern District of Texas and maintains a regular and established place of business at 4100 Innovation Parkway, Suite 220, Plano, Texas 75024, which is within this District.
31	[30] 19.  Defendant has committed acts of infringement in this District by making, using, selling, and offering for sale the PathForge platform to customers located in the Eastern District of Texas. On information and belief, Meridian has actively marketed and sold the PathForge platform to commercial drone operators and enterprises with operations in this District, and Meridian's infringing products have been used and deployed within this District.
32	[31] 20.  Venue is also proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b) and (c) for the non-patent claims asserted herein because a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to SkyVault's claims occurred in this District.
33	[32] IV. FACTUAL BACKGROUND
34	[33] A. SkyVault and Its Innovative UAV Technology
35	[34] 21.  Dr. Rajan Mehta, a former aerospace engineer with extensive experience in avionics, guidance systems, and autonomous vehicle technologies, founded SkyVault Technologies LLC in January 2016 with the mission of developing proprietary UAV flight control and autonomous navigation technology for the commercial drone industry.
36	[35] 22.  Since its founding, SkyVault has invested millions of dollars and years of sustained effort into developing its core technology platform. SkyVault's research and development efforts have produced a comprehensive suite of proprietary technologies, including its flagship "AeroCore" firmware suite, proprietary sensor fusion algorithms, flight path optimization models, drone swarm communication protocols, and hardware integration specifications for advanced sensor arrays.
37	[36] 23.  SkyVault's AeroCore firmware suite is a comprehensive software platform for UAV flight control that integrates multiple proprietary subsystems into a unified autonomous navigation solution. AeroCore enables commercial drones to perform real-time obstacle avoidance, navigate in GPS-denied environments, coordinate multi-drone swarm operations, and interface with a variety of onboard sensor hardware configurations.
38	[37] 24.  SkyVault holds a portfolio of fourteen (14) United States utility patents covering various aspects of its innovative UAV technologies, including the three patents-in-suit described below. SkyVault's patent portfolio is the product of years of intensive research and development by SkyVault's team of engineers and scientists.
39	[38] 25.  SkyVault's proprietary technology provides a significant competitive advantage in the rapidly growing commercial drone market. SkyVault has leveraged its technology to secure contracts with commercial drone operators, logistics companies, agricultural enterprises, and infrastructure inspection firms. SkyVault's success in this market is directly attributable to the innovative technologies it has developed and protected through patents, copyrights, trade secrets, and contractual agreements.
40	[39] 26.  SkyVault employs approximately thirty-four (34) engineers, scientists, and other professionals at its principal place of business in Plano, Texas. SkyVault's team includes experts in aerospace engineering, robotics, embedded systems programming, sensor technology, and artificial intelligence.
41	[40] B. SkyVault's Patents-in-Suit
42	[41] 27.  SkyVault is the owner by assignment of all right, title, and interest in and to the following three United States utility patents, which are asserted in this action:
43	[42] 28.  U.S. Patent No. 10,234,561 (the "'561 Patent"), titled "System and Method for Real-Time Obstacle Avoidance in Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Using Multi-Sensor Fusion," was filed on March 14, 2017, and duly and legally issued on September 18, 2018, by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The '561 Patent has a priority date of March 14, 2017. The '561 Patent contains twenty-two (22) claims, including three (3) independent claims and nineteen (19) dependent claims. The named inventor is Dr. Rajan Mehta. A true and correct copy of the '561 Patent is attached hereto as Exhibit A and incorporated herein by reference.
44	[43] 29.  U.S. Patent No. 10,891,227 (the "'227 Patent"), titled "Adaptive Flight Path Optimization Algorithm for GPS-Denied Environments," was filed on November 9, 2018, and duly and legally issued on January 14, 2020, by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The '227 Patent has a priority date of November 9, 2018. The '227 Patent contains seventeen (17) claims, including two (2) independent claims and fifteen (15) dependent claims. The named inventors are Dr. Rajan Mehta and Dr. Anita Venkatesh. A true and correct copy of the '227 Patent is attached hereto as Exhibit B and incorporated herein by reference.
45	[44] 30.  U.S. Patent No. 11,402,889 (the "'889 Patent"), titled "Low-Latency Communication Protocol for Drone Swarm Coordination," was filed on June 22, 2020, and duly and legally issued on August 2, 2022, by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The '889 Patent has a priority date of June 22, 2020. The '889 Patent contains twenty-eight (28) claims, including four (4) independent claims and twenty-four (24) dependent claims. The named inventors are Dr. Rajan Mehta, Dr. Anita Venkatesh, and Kevin Larsson. A true and correct copy of the '889 Patent is attached hereto as Exhibit C and incorporated herein by reference.
46	[45] 31.  SkyVault is the owner by assignment of all right, title, and interest in and to the '561 Patent, the '227 Patent, and the '889 Patent. SkyVault has standing to assert claims for infringement of each of the patents-in-suit and to seek and recover damages for such infringement.
47	[46] C. SkyVault's AeroCore Firmware and Copyrights
48	[47] 32.  SkyVault developed the AeroCore firmware suite as a comprehensive proprietary software platform for UAV flight control. The AeroCore firmware suite was created by SkyVault employees within the scope of their employment with SkyVault and is owned by SkyVault as a work made for hire under 17 U.S.C. § 201(b).
49	[48] 33.  The AeroCore firmware suite comprises numerous proprietary source code files, including, inter alia, the source code files designated as `navfusion.c`, `pathoptengine.h`, and `swarm_proto.cpp`. These source code files embody SkyVault's proprietary algorithms and methods for sensor fusion, flight path optimization, and drone swarm coordination, respectively.
50	[49] 34.  The AeroCore firmware was developed by SkyVault's engineering team, including during the period of Dr. Holt's employment from 2016 through 2018. The firmware has been continuously refined and updated by SkyVault's engineers since its initial development.
51	[50] 35.  SkyVault's copyright in the AeroCore Firmware Suite is registered with the United States Copyright Office under Registration No. TX 9-142-338, issued on April 3, 2023, covering the "AeroCore Firmware Suite v2.0." A true and correct copy of the copyright registration certificate is attached hereto as Exhibit D and incorporated herein by reference.
52	[51] 36.  The AeroCore firmware suite is a valuable and original work of authorship that reflects SkyVault's substantial creative investment and engineering expertise. SkyVault's copyright in the AeroCore firmware suite is valid and enforceable.

54	[53] 37.  In addition to its patented inventions and copyrighted firmware, SkyVault possesses valuable trade secrets that were developed at great cost and investment over many years and that provide a significant competitive advantage over SkyVault's competitors in the commercial drone market.

IV. RECOMMENDED INTERVIEW SEQUENCE

Recommended order: (1) the Meridian technical team; (2) Dr. Holt; (3) Meridian's legal lead.

First, the technical team. Their testimony sits entirely within Meridian's own privilege, their knowledge is documentary in nature — repositories, test data, release records — and they can identify what exists before anyone's recollection is committed to a version. Retrieval generated by their interviews (commit histories, dependency inventories, test logs) then becomes the objective baseline against which later accounts are measured, which is the highest-value use of an early interview slot.

Second, Dr. Holt. He is the only witness to the 2018 SkyVault-side events — the ECIAA, the exports, the USB transfer, the exit interview — but his account should be taken after the engineering record is assembled, so that his statements about PathForge's origins, public sources, and the white paper can be tested in real time against commit history and test data rather than accepted and revisited. Exhibit F's selected rows (e.g., Rows 27–35) supply the SkyVault-side timeline for the same purpose.

Last, the legal lead. The legal lead's subjects — the correspondence chain, preservation, compliance files — can be confirmed most efficiently once the fact witnesses have identified what records exist, so the preservation and custodial questions can be targeted rather than open-ended. Sequencing this interview last also keeps the privilege boundary cleanest: by then the factual map is drawn, and the interview can be confined to discoverable events (receipt dates, hold dates, custodians) without drifting toward advice or counsel's impressions. Cross-check value runs in both directions at this step: the response letter's assertions of independent development and "robust internal compliance processes" can be tested against what the engineers and Holt actually described, and any gap becomes a concrete retrieval task before the next round.

This order is a recommendation, not the only defensible one: if preservation has not yet been confirmed, the legal lead's preservation questions (C-Q3) should be pulled forward immediately, because hold scope is time-sensitive in a way the other topics are not.

{"path":"/tmp/build_memo.py","content":"# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""Builds /app/output/result.docx — witness-interview outline memorandum."""
import docx
from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, Inches, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement

doc = Document()

# ---------- base styles ----------
normal = doc.styles["Normal"]
normal.font.name = "Times New Roman"
normal.font.size = Pt(11)
normal.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn("w:eastAsia"), "Times New Roman")
pf = normal.paragraph_format
pf.space_after = Pt(6)
pf.line_spacing = 1.15

for s in doc.sections:
    s.top_margin = Inches(1)
    s.bottom_margin = Inches(1)
    s.left_margin = Inches(1)
    s.right_margin = Inches(1)

def para(text="", bold=False, italic=False, align=None, size=None, space_after=6,
         space_before=0, indent=None, color=None):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    r = p.add_run(text)
    r.bold = bold
    r.italic = italic
    if size:
        r.font.size = Pt(size)
    if color:
        r.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(*color)
    if align is not None:
        p.alignment = align
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(space_after)
    p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(space_before)
    if indent is not None:
        p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Inches(indent)
    return p

def rich_para(runs, align=None, space_after=6, space_before=0, indent=None):
    """runs: list of (text, bold, italic)"""
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    for text, bold, italic in runs:
        r = p.add_run(text)
        r.bold = bold
        r.italic = italic
    if align is not None:
        p.alignment = align
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(space_after)
    p.paragraph_format.space_before = Pt(space_before)
    if indent is not None:
        p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Inches(indent)
    return p

def hrule():
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(6)
    pPr = p._p.get_or_add_pPr()
    pBdr = OxmlElement("w:pBdr")
    bottom = OxmlElement("w:bottom")
    bottom.set(qn("w:val"), "single")
    bottom.set(qn("w:sz"), "8")
    bottom.set(qn("w:space"), "1")
    bottom.set(qn("w:color"), "000000")
    pBdr.append(bottom)
    pPr.append(pBdr)
    return p

def h1(text):
    return para(text, bold=True, size=12, space_before=14, space_after=6)

def h2(text):
    return para(text, bold=True, size=11, space_before=10, space_after=4)

def h3(text):
    return para(text, bold=True, italic=True, size=11, space_before=8, space_after=4)

def question(qid, qtext, source, purpose):
    rich_para([(qid + "  ", True, False), (qtext, False, False)],
              space_after=2, indent=0.25)
    rich_para([("Source: ", True, False), (source, False, False)],
              space_after=2, indent=0.55)
    rich_para([("Evidentiary purpose: ", True, False), (purpose, False, False)],
              space_after=8, indent=0.55)

# ---------- caption ----------
para("PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT",
     bold=True, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, size=10, space_after=2)
para("PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION — DO NOT DISTRIBUTE",
     bold=True, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, size=10, space_after=10)
para("MEMORANDUM", bold=True, align=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER, size=14, space_after=10)

rich_para([("TO:\t", True, False),
           ("Engagement Partner, Intellectual Property Litigation Team", False, False)], space_after=2)
rich_para([("FROM:\t", True, False),
           ("Preparing Attorney, Meridian Dynamics Privileged Internal Investigation", False, False)], space_after=2)
rich_para([("DATE:\t", True, False), ("September 20, 2026", False, False)], space_after=2)
rich_para([("RE:\t", True, False),
           ("Witness-Interview Outline and Preparation Memorandum — SkyVault Technologies LLC v. "
            "Meridian Dynamics, Inc., No. 2:24-cv-00817-JRG (E.D. Tex.) — Planned Interviews of "
            "Dr. Marcus Holt, the Meridian Technical Team, and Meridian's Legal Lead", False, False)],
          space_after=4)
hrule()

# ---------- I. purpose ----------
h1("I. PURPOSE, SCOPE, AND LIMITATIONS")
para("This memorandum designs the first round of privileged witness interviews in Meridian Dynamics, "
     "Inc.'s (\u201cMeridian's\u201d) internal fact investigation of the claims asserted by SkyVault "
     "Technologies LLC (\u201cSkyVault\u201d). It is an interview plan only. It is not testimony, a "
     "pleading, a claim chart or infringement analysis, a settlement communication, or an opinion on "
     "the merits. For each of the three witness categories — Dr. Marcus Holt, the Meridian technical "
     "team, and Meridian's legal lead — it states the witness's role in this interview round and then "
     "lists questions that can actually be asked aloud, each annotated with the source document(s) that "
     "generate the lead and the evidentiary purpose the answer would serve.")
para("Only five documents were available in preparing this memorandum: skyvault-complaint.docx; "
     "exhibit-f-forensic-log.xlsx; holt-eciaa-agreement.docx; pathforge-whitepaper-excerpt.docx; and "
     "meridian-cd-response.docx. Personnel files, source code repositories, development and testing "
     "records, preservation and litigation-hold records, internal communications, compliance materials, "
     "the complete forensic data set, and any technical comparison of the accused and asserted "
     "technology are not in the file. Where those missing materials matter, the outlines below convert "
     "them into witness-confirmation questions or document-retrieval requests; nothing here treats them "
     "as established fact. SkyVault's March 12, 2024 letter was not provided; this memorandum attributes "
     "to it only what paragraph 61 of the Complaint and Meridian's April 5, 2024 response letter record.")
para("Interview protocol: questions are drafted in open form because the facts sought require witness "
     "confirmation; interviewers should ask the open question first and use the cited materials for "
     "targeted follow-up rather than leading. Each outline closes with the document and record requests "
     "that the interview is expected to generate.", space_after=10)

# ---------- II. source documents ----------
h1("II. THE FIVE SOURCE DOCUMENTS AND WHAT THEY ACTUALLY ESTABLISH")

h2("A. skyvault-complaint.docx — SkyVault's Original Complaint (filed October 2, 2024)")
para("The Complaint is SkyVault's pleading: its allegations — including those made \u201con information "
     "and belief\u201d (e.g., ¶¶2, 49, 54–55, 59, 118–120) — are claims to be tested, not evidence. Its "
     "value to this investigation is as a map of what SkyVault will try to prove: Holt's employment and "
     "access (¶¶42–47); the alleged February 9, 2018 download of approximately 4,700 files (¶¶48–52); "
     "Meridian's founding and the PathForge platform (¶¶53–60); the pre-suit correspondence (¶¶61–63); "
     "the three asserted patents — the '561, '227, and '889 Patents (¶¶28–30); the AeroCore firmware "
     "copyright, Registration No. TX 9-142-338 (¶¶32–36, 116–121); the five trade-secret categories "
     "TS-1 through TS-5 (¶38); and the ECIAA breach theory (¶¶126–132).")

h2("B. exhibit-f-forensic-log.xlsx — the Exhibit F forensic extract")
para("This is a SkyVault-side extract, not a neutral or complete record. The \u201cReport Metadata\u201d "
     "worksheet states that Hargrove Forensics Group prepared it for SkyVault's counsel (Callister, Voss "
     "& Greenbaum LLP), that the report is dated March 5, 2018, and that the review covered the 'mholt' "
     "account for January 1 – February 28, 2018. Its \u201cNotes\u201d row discloses that the "
     "\u201cForensic Log\u201d worksheet's 50 rows were selected from a full audit population of 12,847 "
     "events. The rows record selected FILE_VIEW, FILE_DOWNLOAD, and BULK_EXPORT events; a USB device "
     "connection and a 4,700-file BULK_COPY_TO_REMOVABLE event (Rows 33–35); and SkyVault IT's response "
     "(Rows 38–50, incident ticket INC-2018-00417). The extract does not by itself establish file "
     "contents, authorization, device ownership, or any subsequent use of the copied files.")

h2("C. holt-eciaa-agreement.docx — the ECIAA (effective June 13, 2016)")
para("The ECIAA is a contract and a prior-inventions disclosure. It establishes the obligations SkyVault "
     "invokes — confidentiality (Section 3, perpetual for trade secrets and three years for other "
     "confidential information), company-systems and personal-device rules (Section 4), invention "
     "assignment with an Exhibit A carve-out (Section 5), and a twelve-month non-solicitation covenant "
     "(Section 7) — and it contains Holt's initialed Exhibit A listing two prior inventions. It does not "
     "by itself establish breach, the scope of Holt's actual access, or anything Holt did after "
     "February 2018.")

h2("D. pathforge-whitepaper-excerpt.docx — the July 2022 public white paper excerpt")
para("The white paper is Meridian's own public technical and marketing statement (title block: "
     "\u201cDocument Classification: Public Release / Marketing Technical Paper\u201d), and the file is "
     "an excerpt of a 42-page paper containing Sections 1–5 and 7 only. It supplies Meridian's public "
     "account of PathForge's development (\u201cDeveloped from the ground up beginning in 2018,\u201d §1; "
     "\u201cAll PathForge technology was developed independently by the Meridian engineering team,\u201d "
     "§7.2), its module architecture (§7.1), its development timeline (§7.2), and its named public "
     "sources (§2; References 1–4). As a party statement it is evidence of what Meridian said publicly; "
     "it is not proof that development in fact occurred as described, and its marketing framing requires "
     "engineering verification.")

h2("E. meridian-cd-response.docx — the April 5, 2024 response letter")
para("This is Meridian's outside-counsel response to the March 12, 2024 demand. Its denials of patent "
     "infringement, trade-secret misappropriation, and copyright infringement; its assertion that "
     "\u201cMeridian independently developed its PathForge platform through the efforts of its "
     "engineering teams\u201d; and its reference to \u201crobust internal compliance processes\u201d are "
     "party positions taken by counsel in a dispute letter. They frame the defenses these interviews must "
     "test; they are not themselves proof of independent development, compliance, non-infringement, or "
     "any other fact.", space_after=10)

# ---------- III. outlines ----------
h1("III. WITNESS-INTERVIEW OUTLINES")

# ===== A. Holt =====
h2("A. Dr. Marcus Holt — former SkyVault Senior Systems Engineer; Meridian co-founder and CTO")
para("Dr. Holt is the central fact witness in this round: SkyVault's allegations run through his "
     "June 2016 – February 2018 employment, his access to SkyVault systems, the February 2018 "
     "file-transfer events, and his co-founding of Meridian two months later (skyvault-complaint.docx "
     "¶¶2, 42–55). He signed the ECIAA and its Exhibit A prior-inventions disclosure, and he is the "
     "named author of the July 2022 white paper whose title and author line SkyVault pleads against "
     "Meridian. Because his potential individual exposure under the ECIAA may diverge from Meridian's "
     "corporate interest, counsel should give appropriate corporate-representation warnings and consider "
     "separate counsel for him before the substantive interview.")

h3("1. Employment and access history")
question("Q-A1.",
    "Please walk me through your time at SkyVault from June 2016 to February 2018 — your title, your "
    "day-to-day duties, the projects you worked on, and the systems and Confluence spaces you used.",
    "skyvault-complaint.docx ¶¶42–44 supplies SkyVault's allegations about Holt's role and the breadth "
    "of his access; holt-eciaa-agreement.docx §1.1 supplies the contractual duty description (research, "
    "development, and engineering of UAV flight control, sensor fusion, and flight path optimization); "
    "exhibit-f-forensic-log.xlsx, \u201cForensic Log\u201d worksheet, Rows 1–32 supplies the recorded "
    "access events (01/03/2018–02/08/2018) to the /SkyVault/Engineering/SensorFusion/, /FlightPath/, "
    "/SwarmProtocol/, /HardwareIntegration/, and /Business/CustomerData/ spaces, all from workstation "
    "SV-ENG-WS-014, IP 10.10.42.118.",
    "Establishes Holt's own account of his authorized access, against which Complaint ¶44's access "
    "allegations can be measured; the log rows corroborate access to engineering spaces but do not "
    "themselves establish what he did with the information, so an open narrative comes first.")
question("Q-A2.",
    "Which of SkyVault's five alleged trade-secret categories — sensor fusion algorithms, flight path "
    "optimization models, customer lists and pricing strategies, swarm communication protocols, and "
    "LiDAR hardware integration specifications — did you actually work with, and which did you never "
    "touch?",
    "skyvault-complaint.docx ¶38 defines TS-1 through TS-5, and ¶44 alleges direct access to TS-1, TS-2, "
    "TS-4, and TS-5 and indirect access to TS-3 through customer demonstrations and proposal "
    "development; exhibit-f-forensic-log.xlsx, \u201cForensic Log\u201d Rows 1–32 supplies the "
    "recorded-access cross-check by Confluence space.",
    "Narrows or confirms the categories genuinely at risk; Holt's category-by-category answer shapes the "
    "misappropriation defense and identifies which allegations rest on inference rather than recorded "
    "access.")
question("Q-A3.",
    "What contact did you have with SkyVault's customer information — for example, customer "
    "demonstrations or proposal work — and do you recall viewing the file "
    "customer_contracts_summary_2017.xlsx on January 24, 2018?",
    "skyvault-complaint.docx ¶44 supplies the TS-3 access allegation; exhibit-f-forensic-log.xlsx, "
    "\u201cForensic Log\u201d Row 17 (01/24/2018, FILE_VIEW, /SkyVault/Business/CustomerData/"
    "customer_contracts_summary_2017.xlsx, Notes: \u201cUser accessed Business/CustomerData space — "
    "outside normal Engineering scope\u201d) and Row 32 (02/08/2018, BULK_EXPORT, 84 files from "
    "/SkyVault/Business/CustomerData/, with a similar note) supply the recorded events.",
    "TS-3 is the only non-technical trade-secret category; this tests whether customer-data access had "
    "an ordinary work explanation or instead supports SkyVault's departure-preparation narrative.")

h3("2. The ECIAA and Holt's disclosed prior work")
question("Q-A4.",
    "What do you remember about negotiating and signing the ECIAA on June 13, 2016, and what did you "
    "understand Sections 3, 4, 5, and 7 to require of you while employed and afterward?",
    "holt-eciaa-agreement.docx §§3.1–3.5 (confidentiality, durations, return of materials), §§4.1–4.4 "
    "(company systems, personal storage devices, monitoring, exit procedures), §§5.1–5.6 (invention "
    "assignment), §7.1 (twelve-month non-solicitation), and the signature page (both parties, "
    "06/13/2016) supply the operative text; skyvault-complaint.docx ¶¶45–47 supplies SkyVault's summary "
    "of the same provisions.",
    "Holt's knowledge and understanding of his contractual obligations bear on the breach-of-contract "
    "count (Count VII) and on willfulness; his answer also frames the §3.4 general-skills-and-knowledge "
    "carve-out he may invoke.")
question("Q-A5.",
    "Tell me about each item you listed on Exhibit A of the ECIAA — the Autonomous Ground Vehicle Path "
    "Planning Algorithm from your 2014–2015 dissertation work, and the RoboNav Sensor Calibration "
    "Toolkit you published on GitHub under an MIT license in 2015. What do they contain, where do they "
    "live today, and did any of that work become part of PathForge?",
    "holt-eciaa-agreement.docx, Exhibit A — Prior Inventions Disclosure (two listed items, initialed "
    "\u201cM.H.,\u201d dated 06/13/2016) supplies the disclosed prior work, read with §5.3 (the Exhibit A "
    "carve-out from assignment); pathforge-whitepaper-excerpt.docx §2 supplies the public continuity of "
    "Holt's academic background as PathForge's stated design basis.",
    "These disclosures pre-date SkyVault and may supply a lawful, documented origin for some PathForge "
    "concepts; the answer identifies retrievable proof (the dissertation, the "
    "github.com/mholt-robotics/robonav-cal repository history) and tests whether PathForge overlaps the "

question("Q-A6.",
    "Before you left SkyVault, did you disclose to SkyVault any inventions you believed you had "
    "conceived during your employment, and was there anything you developed that you believed fell "
    "outside the assignment clause?",
    "holt-eciaa-agreement.docx §5.1 (prompt written disclosure duty), §5.2 (assignment of Company "
    "Inventions), and §5.3 (exclusions) supply the operative obligations; skyvault-complaint.docx "
    "¶128(b) supplies SkyVault's allegation that Holt failed to assign inventions in violation of "
    "Section 5.",
    "Count VII's second breach theory is non-assignment; this locates any disclosure records (missing "

h3("3. The February 2018 events")

    "Walk me through your final two weeks at SkyVault — when you decided to resign, what you told your "

    "February 15, 2018.",

    "What did SkyVault ask of you when you left — at the exit interview or otherwise — and what did you "
    "return, delete, or keep?",
